summary.title: Impact of Chronic Total Occlusion Lesion Length onSix-month Angiographic and 2-year Clinical Outcomes
summary.authors: Jihun Ahn; Byounggeol Choi; Yeon Choi; Jae Kyeong Byun; Ahmed Mashaly; Kareem Abdelshafi; Yoonjee Park; Young Jang; Woohyeun Kim; Eunjin Park; Jin Oh Na; Cheol Ung Choi; Eungju Kim; Chang Gyu Park; Hongseog Seo; Dongjoo Oh; Jinsu Byeon; Sangho Park; Hyeyon Yu; Seung-Woon Rha
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates whether the length of chronic total occlusion (CTO) lesions impacts six-month angiographic and two-year clinical outcomes following successful percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) with drug-eluting stents (DES). A total of 235 consecutive patients were enrolled and divided into long CTO (≥30mm) and short CTO (<30mm) groups. Baseline characteristics were similar except for higher prior PCI in the long group and more bifurcation lesions in the short group. In-hospital complications were comparable, though intimal dissection was more frequent in the long CTO group. At six months, angiographic outcomes, including in-stent restenosis and binary restenosis, were statistically similar between groups, although a numerical trend toward higher restenosis was observed in the long group. Over two years, major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), including death and myocardial infarction, did not differ significantly. However, the incidence of repeat PCI, predominantly target vessel revascularization (TVR), was significantly higher in the long CTO group (18.8% vs. 7.8%). Multivariate analysis identified long CTO as an independent predictor for repeat PCI (OR 4.26). The authors conclude that while long CTO lesions are associated with higher rates of repeat revascularization, they do not translate into worse hard endpoints like mortality or MI, suggesting similar overall safety and efficacy profiles in the DES era.

claims.description: Long CTO lesion length is an independent predictor for repeat PCI.
Angiographic outcomes at 6 months are similar between long and short CTO groups.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates whether the length of chronic total occlusion (CTO) lesions impacts six-month angiographic and two-year clinical outcomes following successful percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) with drug-eluting stents (DES). A total of 235 consecutive patients were enrolled and divided into long CTO (≥30mm) and short CTO (<30mm) groups. Baseline characteristics were similar except for higher prior PCI in the long group and more bifurcation lesions in the short group. In-hospital complications were comparable, though intimal dissection was more frequent in the long CTO group. At six months, angiographic outcomes, including in-stent restenosis and binary restenosis, were statistically similar between groups, although a numerical trend toward higher restenosis was observed in the long group. Over two years, major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), including death and myocardial infarction, did not differ significantly. However, the incidence of repeat PCI, predominantly target vessel revascularization (TVR), was significantly higher in the long CTO group (18.8% vs. 7.8%). Multivariate analysis identified long CTO as an independent predictor for repeat PCI (OR 4.26). The authors conclude that while long CTO lesions are associated with higher rates of repeat revascularization, they do not translate into worse hard endpoints like mortality or MI, suggesting similar overall safety and efficacy profiles in the DES era.

Research Context
Successful CTO PCI is associated with improved clinical outcomes compared to failed PCI. It remains unclear if long CTO lesions have different outcomes than short ones in the DES era. Long coronary artery lesions are known to be worse prognostic factors after PCI. Procedural success rates for CTO patients remain lower than for non-CTO patients. There are no definite answers regarding CTO PCI outcomes based on lesion length.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to investigate if CTO lesion length impacts six-month angiographic outcomes. The study also investigates the impact on two-year clinical outcomes following successful PCI. The authors predicted adverse clinical outcomes would be more frequent in the long CTO group. This prediction was based on worse clinical risk factors in the long CTO group. The use of newer generation DES was dominant in the short CTO group.

Methodological Details
A total of 235 consecutive CTO patients underwent successful PCI with DESs. Patients were enrolled from November 2004 to October 2010 at Korea University Guro Hospital. Patients were divided into long CTO (≥30mm) and short CTO (<30mm) groups. The long CTO group included 159 patients and the short CTO group 76. CTO was defined as complete obstruction with TIMI flow grade 0. The estimated duration of CTO was required to be at least 3 months. Only de novo lesions were included, excluding in-stent restenosis. Loading doses of clopidogrel and aspirin were administered before the index procedure. Maintenance dual antiplatelet therapy included aspirin 100mg and clopidogrel 75mg. Adjunctive cilostazol usage was at the physician's discretion. PCI procedures used standard techniques with various available guidewires. Atheroablative devices were not utilized, and simple pre-dilation was mostly performed. Procedural success was defined as final stenosis less than 30% and TIMI ≥2. Quantitative coronary angiography parameters were measured before, after, and at 6 months. The primary angiographic endpoint was binary restenosis at 6-12 months. Follow-up data was collected via interview, medical records, or telephone. Primary clinical endpoint was MACE, including death, MI, and revascularization. Statistical analysis used Student's t-test, chi-square, and logistic regression.

Procedures And Architectures
PCI was performed using current guidelines and standard techniques. Various guidewires were used to cross the CTO lesion. Simple pre-dilation with balloon was performed to accommodate the stent. Adjunctive balloon dilatation was performed if necessary for optimal outcome. All PCI was performed using DES, with type decided by the operator. QCA measurement and analysis were performed at the Cardiovascular Center. Follow-up angiography was obtained in 99 long CTO and 45 short CTO patients. Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS 20 software. A p-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

Key Results
Baseline characteristics were similar except prior PCI was more frequent in the long group. Bifurcation lesions were more frequent in the short CTO group. Intimal dissection was more frequent in the long CTO group. Total death incidence was 3.1% in long and 5.2% in short groups. Cardiac death incidence was 1.2% in long and 2.6% in short groups. Myocardial infarction incidence was 1.8% in long and 2.6% in short groups. MACE incidence was 21.3% in long and 13.1% in short groups. Repeat PCI incidence was significantly higher in the long CTO group. Target vessel revascularization was 16.3% in long and 6.5% in short groups. Long CTO was an independent predictor for repeat PCI with OR 4.26. In-stent restenosis incidence was 33.3% in long and 26.6% in short groups. Binary restenosis incidence was 19.1% in long and 8.8% in short groups. Late loss was 0.65 mm in long and 0.46 mm in short groups.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Long CTO PCI with DES is similarly safe as short CTO PCI. Higher TVR in long CTO did not translate into increased mortality. Less myocardial viability and developed collaterals may lessen restenosis effects. The study suggests procedural safety and efficacy are similar between groups. Long-term studies with larger populations are needed for final conclusions.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study is not randomized and is a single-center registry. Baseline clinical and procedural characteristics were slightly different between groups. Newer generation DES was more frequent in the short CTO group. Unmeasured confounders and analytical bias could exist despite statistical adjustment. Follow-up angiography was not routinely performed in all patients. The sample size was relatively small, limiting power to detect angiographic differences. The two-year follow-up period was not long enough for long-term safety.

Claims
Long CTO lesion length is an independent predictor for repeat PCI. Multivariate analysis showed long CTO predicted repeat PCI. The odds ratio for repeat PCI was 4.26. Overall MACE rates were not significantly different between groups. Long CTO patients may require closer monitoring for revascularization.
Angiographic outcomes at 6 months are similar between long and short CTO groups. Binary restenosis rates were not statistically different. Late loss values were similar between the two groups. There was a numerical trend toward higher restenosis in the long group. DES implantation provides similar angiographic results regardless of length.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Logistic regression was used to adjust for risk factors. Risk factors included sex, age, hypertension, and diabetes. The study adjusted for prior PCI and bifurcation lesion.

Ethical Considerations
The study protocol was approved by the institutional review board. All patients provided informed consent to participate in the study.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 demonstrates baseline clinical and angiographic characteristics. Table 2 summarizes procedural and in-hospital complications. Table 3 summarizes clinical outcomes for the 2-year follow-up. Table 4 shows predictors for repeat PCI and TVR. Table 5 presents six-month angiographic outcomes.

Three Takeaways
1. Long CTO lesions are associated with higher rates of repeat PCI. 2. Major adverse cardiovascular events were similar between long and short CTO groups. 3. Further long-term studies with larger populations are needed.
